name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q01 - Percentage contribution of plasma in human blood

questiontext.text: Blood is a specialized connective tissue consisting of a fluid matrix, plasma, and formed elements. What percentage of total blood volume is constituted by plasma?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Blood is a specialized fluid connective tissue composed of two major parts: the liquid matrix known as plasma and the cellular components collectively called formed elements.

Step 2: Evaluation of Blood Composition
In healthy human adults, plasma constitutes approximately 55 per cent of the total volume of blood, while formed elements (erythrocytes, leucocytes, and platelets) account for the remaining 45 per cent.

Final Answer: Plasma constitutes nearly 55 per cent of total human blood volume.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q02 - Major protein responsible for blood osmotic balance

questiontext.text: Which major plasma protein plays a primary physiological role in maintaining osmotic balance in human blood?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plasma proteins make up approximately 6 to 8 per cent of plasma. The major proteins include fibrinogens, globulins, and albumins, each serving distinct physiological roles.

Step 2: Evaluation of Protein Functions
Fibrinogens are essential for blood clotting; globulins participate in immune defense mechanisms; and albumins are primarily responsible for maintaining the colloid osmotic balance of blood.

Final Answer: Albumins are the major plasma proteins responsible for maintaining osmotic balance.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q03 - Average lifespan of human red blood cells

questiontext.text: What is the average lifespan of mature human erythrocytes in circulation before they are destroyed in the spleen?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Erythrocytes (red blood cells) are produced in the red bone marrow of adults and lose their nuclei during maturation to maximize room for haemoglobin.

Step 2: Evaluation of RBC Longevity
Lacking nuclei and metabolic repair organelles, human erythrocytes remain functionally active in peripheral circulation for an average lifespan of 120 days. Old and worn-out RBCs are subsequently filtered and destroyed in the spleen.

Final Answer: The average lifespan of human erythrocytes in circulation is 120 days.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q04 - Most abundant white blood cells in blood

questiontext.text: Among the different types of leucocytes present in normal human blood, which cells are the most abundant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Leucocytes (white blood cells) are classified into granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes).

Step 2: Evaluation of Relative Abundance
Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells, representing 60 to 65 per cent of total leucocytes. In contrast, lymphocytes comprise 20 to 25 per cent, monocytes comprise 6 to 8 per cent, eosinophils comprise 2 to 3 per cent, and basophils comprise 0.5 to 1 per cent.

Final Answer: Neutrophils are the most abundant leucocytes, constituting 60 to 65 per cent of total white blood cells.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q05 - Bone marrow precursor cells of blood platelets

questiontext.text: Blood platelets (thrombocytes) are cell fragments produced from which specialized cells in the bone marrow?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Platelets, or thrombocytes, are circulating non-nucleated fragments essential for blood clotting and hemostasis.

Step 2: Evaluation of Origin
Platelets are formed in the red bone marrow by the fragmentation of mature giant precursor cells termed megakaryocytes.

Final Answer: Platelets are cell fragments produced from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q06 - Universal recipient blood group in ABO system

questiontext.text: An individual whose red blood cells carry both antigen A and antigen B, but whose plasma lacks both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, belongs to which ABO blood group?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The ABO blood grouping system relies on the distribution of surface antigens on erythrocytes and natural antibodies in the plasma.

Step 2: Evaluation of Blood Group Characteristics
Group AB erythrocytes display both antigen A and antigen B, while their plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies. Because their plasma does not clump incoming donor RBCs, group AB individuals can receive red blood cells from any ABO group and are termed universal recipients.

Final Answer: Individuals with both antigens A and B on red blood cells and no plasma antibodies belong to blood group AB.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q07 - Heart valve located between left chambers

questiontext.text: Which valve guards the opening between the left atrium and the left ventricle in the human heart?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Atrioventricular valves ensure unidirectional forward flow of blood from the atria into the ventricles and prevent regurgitation during ventricular contraction.

Step 2: Evaluation of Anatomical Location
The opening between the right atrium and right ventricle is guarded by the tricuspid valve, whereas the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle is guarded by the bicuspid valve, also termed the mitral valve.

Final Answer: The bicuspid or mitral valve guards the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q08 - Normal human resting cardiac cycle time duration

questiontext.text: In a healthy human individual with an average resting heart rate of 72 beats per minute, what is the duration of a single cardiac cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A cardiac cycle comprises one complete sequence of contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole) of cardiac chambers.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Calculation
With a resting heart rate of 72 beats per minute (60 seconds), the duration of one cardiac cycle is calculated as \(60\text{ s} / 72 \approx 0.833\text{ s}\), which is standardized in human physiology as 0.8 seconds.

Final Answer: The duration of a single cardiac cycle in a resting healthy human is 0.8 seconds.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q09 - Pumping and resting blood pressure threshold values

questiontext.text: In a standard resting blood pressure reading of \(120/80\text{ mm Hg}\), what do the values 120 and 80 represent respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Arterial blood pressure is recorded as two pressure limits corresponding to ventricular contraction and relaxation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Pressure Limits
The value \(120\text{ mm Hg}\) denotes the systolic pressure, which is the peak pumping pressure during ventricular systole. The value \(80\text{ mm Hg}\) denotes the diastolic pressure, which is the minimum resting pressure maintained during ventricular diastole.

Final Answer: The values 120 and 80 represent systolic (pumping) pressure and diastolic (resting) pressure, respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q10 - Cause of the first prominent heart sound

questiontext.text: During each cardiac cycle, which mechanical event is directly associated with the production of the first heart sound (lub)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The two prominent clinical heart sounds heard with a stethoscope are produced by the closure of specific heart valves.

Step 2: Evaluation of Acoustic Events
The first heart sound (lub) is caused by the simultaneous closure of the atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves at the onset of ventricular systole. In contrast, the second heart sound (dub) corresponds to the closure of the semilunar valves at the onset of ventricular diastole.

Final Answer: The first heart sound (lub) is associated with the closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves.

answer.text: Closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q11 - Definition and composition of human blood serum

questiontext.text: How is blood serum accurately defined in relation to human blood plasma?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plasma contains water, proteins (fibrinogen, globulins, albumins), dissolved nutrients, electrolytes, and factors required for blood coagulation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Serum Composition
When blood clots, fibrinogen and other clotting factors are consumed in forming the insoluble fibrin meshwork. The remaining clear straw-colored fluid that separates from the clot is plasma devoid of clotting factors, defined as serum.

Final Answer: Serum is defined as plasma without the clotting factors.

answer.text: Whole blood without formed elements and glucose
Fluid matrix containing only fibrinogen and platelets

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q12 - Secretory products and role of basophil granulocytes

questiontext.text: Which substances are secreted by basophils during inflammatory reactions in the human body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Basophils are granulocytes with coarse granules that play critical roles in inflammatory and allergic reactions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Secretory Products
Basophils secrete chemical mediators including histamine (a vasodilator), serotonin (a vasoconstrictor), and heparin (an anticoagulant), all of which participate in mediating inflammatory reactions.

Final Answer: Basophils secrete histamine, serotonin, and heparin during inflammatory reactions.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q13 - Primary immune function of eosinophil granulocytes

questiontext.text: What are the primary physiological roles associated with eosinophils in human peripheral blood?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Eosinophils are granulocytes with bilobed nuclei and prominent cytoplasmic granules that take up acidic stains, constituting 2 to 3 per cent of total white blood cells.

Step 2: Evaluation of Functional Roles
Eosinophils function primarily in resisting parasitic infections and are characteristically elevated during and associated with allergic reactions.

Final Answer: Eosinophils function to resist infections and are associated with allergic reactions.

answer.text: Resisting infections and participating in allergic reactions

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q14 - Major phagocytic cells among human white leucocytes

questiontext.text: Which types of leucocytes function actively as phagocytic cells to destroy foreign organisms entering the human body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phagocytosis is an innate defense mechanism in which specialized white blood cells engulf and digest foreign microbes and cellular debris.

Step 2: Evaluation of Phagocytic Leucocytes
Among circulating leucocytes, neutrophils (granulocytes constituting 60 to 65 per cent) and monocytes (agranulocytes constituting 6 to 8 per cent) are phagocytic cells that engulf and destroy invading microorganisms.

Final Answer: Neutrophils and monocytes are the major phagocytic cells that destroy foreign organisms.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q15 - Sequential enzymatic steps in blood clot formation

questiontext.text: In the cascade mechanism of blood coagulation, which enzyme is directly responsible for converting inactive soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Blood coagulation involves an enzyme cascade where inactive precursors are sequentially converted into active enzymes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Cascade Steps
The enzyme complex thrombokinase activates inactive prothrombin into thrombin. Thrombin then acts directly as the proteolytic enzyme that converts soluble fibrinogen in plasma into insoluble fibrin threads to form the clot coagulum.

Final Answer: Thrombin directly converts inactive fibrinogen into active fibrin threads.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q16 - Essential divalent mineral cation in blood coagulation

questiontext.text: Which mineral cation plays an essential and indispensable role at multiple stages in the cascade mechanism of blood clotting?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The blood clotting cascade requires specific mineral cofactors to facilitate enzymic conversions and complex assemblies.

Step 2: Evaluation of Ion Function
Calcium ions (\(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\)) are required as an essential cofactor for the activation of clotting factors, including the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin and subsequent polymerization of fibrin.

Final Answer: Calcium ions play a critical and indispensable role in blood clotting.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q17 - Medical prevention of erythroblastosis foetalis condition

questiontext.text: How can the development of erythroblastosis foetalis be prevented in an Rh-negative mother delivering an Rh-positive newborn?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During delivery of an Rh-positive infant, foetal erythrocytes can leak into maternal Rh-negative blood, stimulating the mother's immune system to produce anti-Rh antibodies that threaten subsequent Rh-positive pregnancies.

Step 2: Evaluation of Prophylaxis
This sensitization is prevented by administering exogenous anti-Rh antibodies (Rh-immunoglobulin) to the mother immediately after the delivery of the first child, destroying any entered foetal Rh-positive RBCs before maternal immune memory is triggered.

Final Answer: Erythroblastosis foetalis is prevented by administering anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after the delivery of the first child.

answer.text: Administering anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after delivery of the first child
Administering Rh antigens to the mother prior to her subsequent pregnancy
Transfusing Rh-positive whole blood to the mother during early gestation
Providing immunosuppressive drugs to the foetus during the final trimester

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q18 - ABO blood group compatibility for safe transfusion

questiontext.text: A recipient with blood group B requires an urgent blood transfusion. From which donor blood groups can this individual safely receive blood?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A recipient cannot receive donor red blood cells that possess surface antigens against which the recipient carries plasma antibodies.

Step 2: Evaluation of Compatibility
An individual with blood group B has antigen B on erythrocytes and anti-A antibodies in plasma. Blood from group B donors (having antigen B) and group O donors (having no ABO surface antigens) will not react with the recipient's anti-A antibodies and can be safely transfused.

Final Answer: A group B recipient can safely receive blood from group B and group O donors.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q19 - Structural composition and origin of interstitial tissue fluid

questiontext.text: How does the composition of interstitial fluid (tissue fluid) differ from that of circulating blood plasma?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
As blood flows through capillaries, hydrostatic pressure forces water and small solutes into intercellular spaces, while continuous capillary walls retain large molecules and cells.

Step 2: Evaluation of Interstitial Fluid Features
Interstitial fluid contains the same mineral distribution as plasma and facilitates nutrient and gas exchange, but it is largely devoid of larger plasma proteins and formed elements, which remain inside capillary vessels.

Final Answer: Interstitial fluid lacks larger plasma proteins and most formed elements while retaining a mineral distribution identical to plasma.

answer.text: It contains higher concentrations of fibrinogen and red blood cells than plasma
It lacks larger plasma proteins and most formed elements but has a similar mineral distribution
It is completely devoid of dissolved glucose, amino acids, and minerals
It contains higher albumin concentration and lower water content than plasma

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q20 - Specialized lymphatic vessels for intestinal lipid absorption

questiontext.text: Through which specialized lymphatic vessels are dietary fats absorbed in the human intestinal villi?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dietary lipids are emulsified and digested into micelles in the small intestine, resynthesized into chylomicrons inside enterocytes, and absorbed into the lymphatic network.

Step 2: Evaluation of Lymphatic Structures
In the intestinal villi, specialized blind-ended central lymphatic capillaries known as lacteals absorb chylomicrons and transport fatty lymph into the lymphatic circulation.

Final Answer: Dietary fats are absorbed through lacteals present in the intestinal villi.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q21 - Vertebrate groups exhibiting incomplete double circulation pattern

questiontext.text: In which groups of vertebrates does the heart pump out mixed blood from a single ventricle, exhibiting incomplete double circulation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Vertebrate hearts exhibit evolutionary adaptations: fishes have a 2-chambered heart (single circulation); amphibians and reptiles have 3 chambers (incomplete double circulation); birds and mammals have 4 chambers (complete double circulation).

Step 2: Evaluation of 3-Chambered Heart
Amphibians and reptiles (with the exception of crocodiles) possess a 3-chambered heart with two atria and a single ventricle. Oxygenated blood from respiratory organs and deoxygenated blood from the body enter separate atria but mix within the single ventricle before being pumped out.

Final Answer: Amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles) exhibit incomplete double circulation with mixed ventricular blood.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q22 - Natural anatomical pacemaker of the human heart

questiontext.text: Why is the sino-atrial node (SAN) designated as the natural pacemaker of the human heart?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cardiac nodal tissue is autoexcitable, meaning it spontaneously generates action potentials without external neurogenic stimulation.

Step 2: Evaluation of SAN Properties
Although multiple regions of the nodal system can generate action potentials, the sino-atrial node (SAN) generates the highest frequency of action potentials (70 to 75 per minute). Consequently, it dictates the rhythm of atrial and ventricular contractions and sets the pace for the entire heart.

Final Answer: The sino-atrial node is called the pacemaker because it generates the maximum number of action potentials (70 to 75 per minute) to set the cardiac pace.

answer.text: It conducts impulses directly into the ventricular myocardium without delay
It generates the maximum number of action potentials (\(70\text{--}75\text{ min}^{-1}\)) to set the cardiac pace
It has the thickest muscular myocardium among all cardiac chambers
It contracts with greater mechanical force than ventricular muscle

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q23 - Percentage increment in ventricular filling during atrial systole

questiontext.text: During the resting human cardiac cycle, by approximately what percentage does atrial systole increase the flow of blood into the ventricles?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During joint diastole, blood flows passively from the great veins through the open atrioventricular valves into the ventricles, filling the majority of ventricular capacity.

Step 2: Evaluation of Atrial Contraction
Simultaneous contraction of both atria (atrial systole) following an action potential from the sino-atrial node squeezes the remaining blood into the ventricles, increasing ventricular blood flow by approximately 30 per cent.

Final Answer: Atrial systole increases the flow of blood into the ventricles by about 30 per cent.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q24 - Electrical conduction pathway across the human myocardium

questiontext.text: What is the correct anatomical pathway for the conduction of cardiac action potentials through the human heart?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An orderly sequence of electrical excitation is essential for synchronized contraction of atria followed by ventricles.

Step 2: Evaluation of Conduction Pathway
The impulse originates in the sino-atrial node (SAN) in the right atrium, travels to the atrio-ventricular node (AVN), continues through the atrio-ventricular bundle (AV bundle / bundle of His), divides into right and left bundle branches, and spreads throughout the ventricular myocardium via Purkinje fibres.

Final Answer: The conduction sequence is Sino-atrial node \(\rightarrow\) Atrio-ventricular node \(\rightarrow\) Atrio-ventricular bundle \(\rightarrow\) Purkinje fibres.

answer.text: Sino-atrial node \(\rightarrow\) Atrio-ventricular node \(\rightarrow\) Atrio-ventricular bundle \(\rightarrow\) Purkinje fibres
Atrio-ventricular node \(\rightarrow\) Sino-atrial node \(\rightarrow\) Purkinje fibres \(\rightarrow\) AV bundle
Sino-atrial node \(\rightarrow\) Purkinje fibres \(\rightarrow\) AV bundle \(\rightarrow\) Atrio-ventricular node
Atrio-ventricular bundle \(\rightarrow\) Sino-atrial node \(\rightarrow\) Atrio-ventricular node \(\rightarrow\) Purkinje fibres

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q25 - Calculation of human cardiac output from resting parameters

questiontext.text: If a healthy adult individual has a resting heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of \(70\text{ mL}\) per beat, what is the total cardiac output?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Resting heart rate (\(\text{HR}\)) is 70 beats per minute. Stroke volume (\(\text{SV}\)) pumped by each ventricle per contraction is \(70\text{ mL}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Cardiac output (\(\text{CO}\)) is defined as the volume of blood pumped out by each ventricle per minute, given by the formula: \[\text{CO} = \text{Stroke Volume} \times \text{Heart Rate}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the equation: \[\text{CO} = 70\text{ mL/beat} \times 70\text{ beats/min} = 4900\text{ mL min}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The units are volume per unit time (\(\text{mL min}^{-1}\)), which is consistent with resting physiological cardiac output of approximately 5 litres per minute.

Final Answer: The cardiac output is \(4900\text{ mL min}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q26 - Electrical depolarization represented by standard ECG P wave

questiontext.text: In a standard electrocardiogram (ECG), what physiological event is represented by the P-wave?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An electrocardiogram is a graphic recording of the electrical potentials generated by cardiac muscle during each cardiac cycle.

Step 2: Evaluation of Waveforms
The P-wave represents the electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, which spreads from the sino-atrial node across the atrial musculature and leads directly to atrial contraction (atrial systole).

Final Answer: The P-wave represents the depolarisation of both atria.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q27 - Physiological event represented by the ECG QRS complex

questiontext.text: In a standard electrocardiogram, what does the QRS complex represent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The QRS complex is the most prominent deflection in a standard electrocardiogram recording.

Step 2: Evaluation of Ventricular Activation
The QRS complex corresponds to the depolarisation of the ventricles as the action potential sweeps through the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres. Ventricular contraction begins shortly after the Q wave and marks the onset of ventricular systole.

Final Answer: The QRS complex represents the depolarisation of the ventricles.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q28 - Physiological significance of the ECG T wave

questiontext.text: In a standard electrocardiogram, what does the T-wave signify, and what event does its termination mark?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Following muscular excitation and contraction, cardiac myocytes must repolarise back to their resting membrane potential before another contraction can occur.

Step 2: Evaluation of Repolarisation Phase
The T-wave represents the repolarisation of the ventricles, reflecting the return of ventricular musculature from an excited state to a resting state. The conclusion of the T-wave clinically marks the end of ventricular systole.

Final Answer: The T-wave signifies ventricular repolarisation, and its end marks the end of systole.

answer.text: Depolarisation of the ventricles; beginning of ventricular systole
Repolarisation of the ventricles; end of ventricular systole
Repolarisation of the atria; end of atrial systole
Depolarisation of the atria; beginning of atrial systole

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q29 - Histological difference in tunica media between blood vessels

questiontext.text: How does the tunica media of a vein structurally compare to that of an artery of similar caliber?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Arteries and veins share a three-layered vascular wall: an inner tunica intima of squamous endothelium, a middle tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibres, and an outer tunica externa of fibrous collagenous connective tissue.

Step 2: Evaluation of Structural Differences
Arteries withstand high, pulsating systemic pressures and therefore possess a well-developed, thick tunica media. Veins operate under lower hydrostatic pressure and feature a comparatively thinner tunica media with a wider central lumen.

Final Answer: The tunica media of a vein is comparatively thinner than that of an artery.

answer.text: It is comparatively thinner with less smooth muscle and elastic fibres
It is comparatively thicker with dense multi-layered smooth muscle
It is composed of stratified squamous epithelium instead of muscle
It contains dense collagen fibres but completely lacks elastic tissue

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q30 - Vascular pathway of the human hepatic portal system

questiontext.text: What vascular connection constitutes the hepatic portal system in the human body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A portal system is a vascular arrangement where capillary beds of one organ drain into a portal vein that breaks into a second capillary bed before returning blood to the heart.

Step 2: Evaluation of Hepatic Portal Route
In humans, the hepatic portal vein collects nutrient-rich venous blood from the capillary beds of the intestine and conveys it directly to the liver sinusoids before it enters the systemic circulation via the hepatic veins and inferior vena cava.

Final Answer: The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver before systemic delivery.

answer.text: Hepatic vein carries oxygenated blood directly from the aorta to the liver

Hepatic artery drains deoxygenated blood from the liver into the inferior vena cava
Celiac trunk delivers deoxygenated blood directly from the pancreas to the kidneys

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q31 - Sympathetic nervous system effects on heart function

questiontext.text: How do neural signals transmitted through sympathetic nerves influence cardiac activity?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The autonomic nervous system regulates heart function through sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions controlled by a cardiac center in the medulla oblongata.

Step 2: Evaluation of Sympathetic Influence
Sympathetic nerves release noradrenaline, which accelerates the firing rate of the sino-atrial node, increases the contractility of the ventricular myocardium, and consequently elevates both heart rate and cardiac output.

Final Answer: Sympathetic signals increase heart rate, the strength of ventricular contraction, and cardiac output.

answer.text: Increase heart rate, increase strength of ventricular contraction, and increase cardiac output

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q32 - Pathological features of coronary artery disease atherosclerosis

questiontext.text: Coronary Artery Disease (CAD), often termed atherosclerosis, is primarily caused by the deposition of which substances within arterial walls?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Coronary artery disease reduces the functional caliber of vessels that supply oxygenated blood and nutrients to the cardiac muscle tissue.

Step 2: Evaluation of Pathological Deposits
Atherosclerosis develops due to luminal narrowing caused by progressive subendothelial deposits of calcium, lipids/fats, cholesterol, and fibrous tissue within the coronary arteries.

Final Answer: Atherosclerosis is caused by deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol, and fibrous tissues.

answer.text: Amyloid fibrils, glycogen granules, and hyaluronic acid
Urea, uric acid, and calcium oxalate stones

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q33 - Clinical presentation and physiological basis of angina pectoris

questiontext.text: What is the primary underlying cause of the acute chest pain experienced during an episode of angina pectoris?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Myocardial cells require a continuous supply of oxygenated blood to synthesize ATP for unceasing rhythmic contractions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Angina Mechanism
When blood flow through coronary vessels is compromised, insufficient oxygen reaches the myocardium to meet its metabolic demands. This myocardial ischemia triggers acute referred chest pain, clinically designated as angina pectoris.

Final Answer: Angina pectoris occurs when insufficient oxygen reaches the heart muscle.

answer.text: Sudden cessation of action potential generation by the sino-atrial node
Excessive accumulation of tissue fluid in alveolar spaces of the lungs
Mechanical rupture of chordae tendineae attached to the atrioventricular valves

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q34 - Heart sound associated with semilunar valve closure

questiontext.text: Which acoustic event in the heart is directly responsible for producing the second heart sound (dub)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The cardiac cycle produces two distinct acoustic vibrations perceptible through auscultation with a stethoscope.

Step 2: Evaluation of Sound Origin
As ventricular diastole begins, pressure in the ventricles drops lower than arterial pressure in the pulmonary artery and aorta. The attempted backward surge of blood forces the pocket-like flaps of the semilunar valves to close abruptly, generating the sharp second heart sound (dub).

Final Answer: The second heart sound (dub) is associated with the closure of the semilunar valves.

answer.text: Closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves at the beginning of systole
Closure of the semilunar valves at the onset of ventricular diastole
Rapid opening of the aortic valve during rapid ventricular ejection
Opening of the atrioventricular valves during joint diastole

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q35 - Quantitative calculation of athlete stroke volume and output

questiontext.text: A trained endurance athlete at rest exhibits a resting heart rate of 50 beats per minute and a resting cardiac output of \(6.0\text{ L min}^{-1}\). What is the stroke volume pumped by each ventricle per cardiac cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Heart rate (\(\text{HR}\)) = 50 beats per minute. Cardiac output (\(\text{CO}\)) = \(6.0\text{ L min}^{-1} = 6000\text{ mL min}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Cardiac output represents stroke volume (\(\text{SV}\)) multiplied by heart rate: \[\text{CO} = \text{SV} \times \text{HR} \implies \text{SV} = \frac{\text{CO}}{\text{HR}}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate stroke volume by substituting the resting values: \[\text{SV} = \frac{6000\text{ mL min}^{-1}}{50\text{ beats min}^{-1}} = 120\text{ mL/beat}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Athletes have physiological ventricular hypertrophy, giving them a significantly higher resting stroke volume (\(120\text{ mL}\)) than sedentary individuals (approximately \(70\text{ mL}\)).

Final Answer: The stroke volume pumped per cardiac cycle is \(120\text{ mL}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q36 - Clinical differentiation among heart failure arrest and attack

questiontext.text: Which of the following descriptions accurately distinguishes heart failure from cardiac arrest and myocardial infarction (heart attack)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different circulatory disorders reflect distinct anatomical and physiological dysfunctions of the heart.

Step 2: Evaluation of Pathologies
Heart failure designates the pathological state where the heart cannot pump sufficient blood to meet bodily metabolic needs (often leading to pulmonary congestion). Cardiac arrest describes the sudden cessation of all electrical and mechanical heart beats. Myocardial infarction (heart attack) denotes sudden ischemic necrosis of cardiac muscle tissue resulting from inadequate coronary blood perfusion.

Final Answer: Heart failure is inadequate pumping meeting bodily needs, cardiac arrest is cessation of heart beat, and a heart attack is sudden myocardial damage from deficient blood supply.

answer.text: Heart failure is the state where the heart does not pump blood effectively to meet metabolic needs; cardiac arrest is when the heart stops beating; a heart attack is sudden damage to heart muscle by inadequate blood supply
Heart failure is when the heart completely stops beating; cardiac arrest is pulmonary congestion; a heart attack is chronic arterial plaque deposition
Heart failure is acute chest pain from oxygen deprivation; cardiac arrest is valvular incompetence; a heart attack is loss of sino-atrial node autoexcitability
Heart failure is rupture of the inter-ventricular septum; cardiac arrest is elevated systolic pressure; a heart attack is systemic arteriolar vasodilation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q37 - Quantitative evaluation of total blood haemoglobin content

questiontext.text: A healthy adult male has a total circulating blood volume of 5 litres and a haemoglobin concentration of \(14\text{ g}\) per \(100\text{ mL}\) of blood. What is the total mass of haemoglobin present in his entire circulatory system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total blood volume = \(5\text{ L} = 5000\text{ mL}\). Haemoglobin concentration = \(14\text{ g}\) per \(100\text{ mL}\) of blood.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Total haemoglobin mass is given by: \[\text{Total Mass} = \text{Concentration} \times \text{Total Volume}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Determine the number of \(100\text{ mL}\) increments in 5000 mL: \[\frac{5000\text{ mL}}{100\text{ mL}} = 50\] Multiply by the haemoglobin content per 100 mL: \[50 \times 14\text{ g} = 700\text{ g}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
A total haemoglobin content of 700 grams in 5 litres of blood is physically sound and aligns with normal Class 11 physiology ranges.

Final Answer: The total mass of haemoglobin in the entire circulation is \(700\text{ g}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q38 - Mechanism of maternal sensitization in erythroblastosis foetalis

questiontext.text: Why does erythroblastosis foetalis generally NOT affect the first Rh-positive child born to an Rh-negative mother, but poses a severe risk in subsequent Rh-positive pregnancies?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Immune sensitization requires initial exposure to a foreign antigen followed by clonal expansion and production of memory B cells and specific antibodies.

Step 2: Evaluation of Immunological Mechanism
During the first pregnancy, the placenta forms an intact barrier keeping foetal Rh-positive RBCs separate from maternal Rh-negative blood. During parturition of the first child, minor feto-maternal hemorrhage occurs, exposing maternal lymphocytes to Rh antigens and inducing anti-Rh antibody production. In subsequent pregnancies with an Rh-positive foetus, maternal anti-Rh IgG antibodies cross the placenta into foetal circulation, destroying foetal red blood cells.

Final Answer: Maternal and foetal blood remain separated during first gestation, but delivery causes exposure that induces maternal antibodies, which can cross the placenta in subsequent pregnancies.

answer.text: Maternal and foetal blood are separated by the placenta during pregnancy, but delivery exposes maternal blood to Rh antigens, inducing antibodies that cross the placenta in subsequent pregnancies
The first foetus secretes immunosuppressive proteins that eliminate maternal memory lymphocytes
Rh antigens only synthesize on foetal erythrocytes starting from the second pregnancy onward
Maternal anti-Rh antibodies are restricted exclusively to the large pentameric IgM class in all gestations

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q39 - Pressure changes and valvular actions in ventricular systole

questiontext.text: During the initial phase of ventricular systole, before intraventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure, what mechanical and valvular events take place within the heart?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ventricular contraction causes a rapid surge in intraventricular pressure, influencing atrioventricular and semilunar valves depending on pressure gradients across them.

Step 2: Evaluation of Mechanical Sequence
As ventricular systole initiates, the rising ventricular pressure instantly exceeds atrial pressure. This causes backward blood movement that forces the tricuspid and bicuspid valves shut. Because ventricular pressure has not yet surpassed pressure in the pulmonary artery and aorta, the semilunar valves remain closed, resulting in isovolumetric contraction.

Final Answer: Ventricular pressure rises, closing the atrioventricular valves while semilunar valves remain closed.

answer.text: Ventricular pressure rises sharply, causing immediate closure of the atrioventricular valves while semilunar valves remain closed
Ventricular pressure declines, pulling open the tricuspid and bicuspid valves
Both atrioventricular and semilunar valves open simultaneously to release blood
Semilunar valves open immediately before atrioventricular valves close

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q40 - Contrasting physiological advantages of closed circulatory systems

questiontext.text: Why is a closed circulatory system (as found in annelids and chordates) considered physiologically more advantageous than an open circulatory system (as found in arthropods and molluscs)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Circulatory systems evolved from open hemolymph sinuses to confined, pressurized vascular conduits.

Step 2: Evaluation of Closed System Advantages
In an open system, blood is pumped into open sinuses where pressure drops and distribution cannot be adjusted selectively. In a closed system, blood remains confined within distinct muscular vessels, allowing high pressure, rapid velocity, and precise neurohumoral regulation of blood flow to specific tissues according to metabolic demands.

Final Answer: A closed circulatory system is more advantageous because blood flow can be precisely regulated and directed to specific organs.

answer.text: Blood flow and pressure can be more precisely regulated and directed to specific metabolically active tissues
Blood pressure remains constant and uniform in all internal body cavities
It completely eliminates the physiological requirement of respiratory pigments for oxygen transport
Circulating fluid directly bathes every tissue cell without needing capillary endothelia

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q41 - Determination of heart rate from standard ECG strip

questiontext.text: A clinical monitor records a continuous 10-second standard electrocardiogram (ECG) strip from a patient and displays exactly 15 QRS complexes. What is the patient's estimated resting heart rate in beats per minute?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Time duration of recording = 10 seconds. Number of QRS complexes counted = 15.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Each QRS complex corresponds to one ventricular depolarisation and subsequent ventricular contraction (one heartbeat). The heart rate in beats per minute (bpm) is determined by extrapolating the count to a 60-second interval: \[\text{Heart Rate} = \text{Number of complexes in 10 s} \times \left(\frac{60\text{ s}}{10\text{ s}}\right)\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Multiply the counted complexes by 6: \[\text{Heart Rate} = 15 \times 6 = 90\text{ beats min}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The calculated rate of 90 beats per minute represents a normal physiological adult heart rate.

Final Answer: The patient's heart rate is 90 beats per minute.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q42 - Analysis of donor and recipient blood group compatibility

questiontext.text: An emergency patient with blood group O negative (\(\mathrm{O^{-}}\)) requires an immediate packed red blood cell transfusion. Which donor blood group can be safely transfused into this patient?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Safe blood transfusion requires matching both ABO antigens and Rh antigens to avoid antigen-antibody clumping (hemolysis).

Step 2: Evaluation of Compatibility
An individual with blood group \(\mathrm{O^{-}}\) lacks A, B, and Rh antigens on red blood cells, and possesses circulating anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma. Transfusing blood with A, B, or Rh antigens will trigger immune-mediated destruction of donor erythrocytes. Therefore, only blood lacking all three antigens (\(\mathrm{O^{-}}\)) can be safely administered.

Final Answer: A patient with blood group O negative can safely receive only O negative blood.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q43 - Functional interplay of intrinsic nodal autoexcitability

questiontext.text: Although both the atrio-ventricular node (AVN) and Purkinje fibres possess intrinsic autoexcitability, why does the sino-atrial node (SAN) normally drive and set the heart rate of the human heart?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Various components of the cardiac nodal system have spontaneous diastolic depolarization capabilities, but the component with the highest firing frequency overrides slower pacemaker sites.

Step 2: Evaluation of Nodal Hierarchy
The sino-atrial node spontaneously depolarizes at the fastest inherent rate (70 to 75 action potentials per minute), whereas the AVN (40 to 60 per minute) and Purkinje fibres (20 to 40 per minute) are slower. Impulses from the SAN conduct across the heart and depolarize downstream nodal tissues before they can spontaneously reach threshold, thereby pacing the whole heart.

Final Answer: The sino-atrial node sets the heart rate because it possesses the highest intrinsic frequency of action potential generation.

answer.text: The sino-atrial node possesses the highest intrinsic frequency of action potential generation, depolarizing other nodal tissues before they reach threshold spontaneously
The atrio-ventricular node and Purkinje fibres lack voltage-gated ion channels necessary for rhythmicity
Sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves exclusively innervate the sino-atrial node without contacting downstream nodes
The fibrous atrioventricular septum completely prevents electrical conductivity from reaching the ventricles

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q44 - Contrasting parasympathetic and sympathetic modulation of cardiac output

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the contrasting regulatory effects of parasympathetic neural signals versus adrenal medullary hormones on human cardiac activity?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Extrinsic regulation of cardiac activity involves opposing autonomic neural inputs and endocrine hormones.

Step 2: Evaluation of Regulatory Mechanisms
Parasympathetic neural signals (via the vagus nerve) release acetylcholine, which decreases the rate of heartbeat, diminishes the speed of conduction of action potentials, and reduces cardiac output. In contrast, adrenal medullary hormones (adrenaline and noradrenaline) stimulate cardiac tissue, increasing the heart rate, myocardial contractility, and cardiac output.

Final Answer: Parasympathetic signals decrease heart rate and conduction speed, whereas adrenal medullary hormones increase heart rate and cardiac output.

Parasympathetic signals increase ventricular contractility, whereas adrenal medullary hormones decrease cardiac output

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q45 - Detailed biochemical cascade of blood thrombokinase activation

questiontext.text: In the cascade mechanism of blood coagulation, what is the specific biochemical role of the enzyme complex thrombokinase?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hemostasis relies on a multi-step enzymatic amplification cascade in which inactive zymogens are converted into active proteases.

Step 2: Evaluation of Cascade Reactions
Tissue trauma and platelet activation trigger a series of linked enzymatic reactions involving inactive plasma factors, culminating in the assembly of the thrombokinase complex (prothrombinase). Thrombokinase, in the presence of calcium ions, catalyzes the proteolytic cleavage of inactive prothrombin into active thrombin.

Final Answer: Thrombokinase catalyzes the conversion of inactive prothrombin into active thrombin.

Hydrolyzing circulating albumins to liberate calcium ions into injured tissues

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q46 - Distribution of blood volume pumped by human ventricles

questiontext.text: During a single resting cardiac cycle in a healthy individual, what volume of blood is pumped by the right ventricle into the pulmonary circulation, and what volume is pumped by the left ventricle into the systemic circulation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a complete double circulatory system, the pulmonary and systemic circuits operate in series.

Step 2: Evaluation of Ventricular Stroke Volumes
To maintain hemodynamic equilibrium and prevent fluid pooling in either pulmonary or systemic vascular beds, both ventricles must pump equal volumes of blood with each contraction. During each cardiac cycle, the right ventricle ejects approximately \(70\text{ mL}\) (stroke volume) into the pulmonary artery, and the left ventricle ejects approximately \(70\text{ mL}\) into the aorta.

Final Answer: Both the right ventricle and the left ventricle pump approximately \(70\text{ mL}\) of blood per cycle.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q47 - Diagnostic criteria and clinical sequelae of chronic hypertension

questiontext.text: Repeated clinical blood pressure measurements of a patient consistently show \(150/95\text{ mm Hg}\). What is the clinical diagnosis, and which vital organs are most susceptible to long-term pathological damage from this condition?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Normal resting blood pressure is \(120/80\text{ mm Hg}\). Chronic elevation of blood pressure exceeding defined thresholds produces target organ damage.

Step 2: Evaluation of Clinical Status
A consistent blood pressure of \(140/90\text{ mm Hg}\) or higher defines hypertension. Sustained elevated vascular pressure damages microvasculature and end-organs, predisposing the patient to heart disease, cerebrovascular accidents (stroke in the brain), and renal damage (kidney failure).

Final Answer: The diagnosis is hypertension, and the vital organs most severely affected are the brain and kidney.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_MCQ_Q48 - Complete pathway of pulmonary and systemic double circulation

questiontext.text: Which sequence correctly traces the complete circuit of deoxygenated blood leaving systemic tissues until it is delivered as oxygenated blood back to the systemic capillaries?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Human circulation is a complete double circulation comprising two distinct circuits: the pulmonary circuit for gas exchange and the systemic circuit for tissue delivery.

Step 2: Evaluation of Circulatory Route
Deoxygenated blood collected from tissues travels through the vena cava into the right atrium, passes into the right ventricle, and is pumped via the pulmonary artery to the lungs. After oxygenation, blood is carried by pulmonary veins to the left atrium, moves into the left ventricle, and is pumped through the aorta into systemic capillary beds.

Final Answer: The correct pathway is Vena cava \(\rightarrow\) Right atrium \(\rightarrow\) Right ventricle \(\rightarrow\) Pulmonary artery \(\rightarrow\) Lungs \(\rightarrow\) Pulmonary veins \(\rightarrow\) Left atrium \(\rightarrow\) Left ventricle \(\rightarrow\) Aorta.

Vena cava \(\rightarrow\) Left atrium \(\rightarrow\) Left ventricle \(\rightarrow\) Pulmonary artery \(\rightarrow\) Lungs \(\rightarrow\) Pulmonary veins \(\rightarrow\) Right atrium \(\rightarrow\) Right ventricle \(\rightarrow\) Aorta
